title: 5 Great Summer Books For Teachers
author: Michael Linsin
summary: In a departure from his usual how-to format, Linsin shares five books from his personal library that he says shaped his thinking on teaching and classroom management, explaining first that he deliberately avoids reading professional education books so his own writing stays based purely on firsthand classroom experience. The five picks — The Oxygen Advantage, Improv Wisdom, Flow, Essentialism, and Peak — are each given several sentences of personal reflection on how the book affected his teaching, his energy, or his understanding of student motivation, rather than a bare citation. He connects Flow, for instance, directly to his rejection of extrinsic rewards, and Essentialism to how he now audits his own use of time. He closes by inviting readers to share their own favorite non-teaching summer reads in the comments.
points: Linsin deliberately avoids reading professional teaching books to keep his own writing based purely on firsthand classroom experience.
The Oxygen Advantage's breathing techniques improved his fitness and exercise performance, not just relaxation.
Flow directly shaped his rejection of extrinsic rewards and his understanding of intrinsic student motivation.
Essentialism prompted him to audit how he spends his time and double down on what matters most.
Peak argues that how a skill is practiced, not just effort alone, determines whether students become excellent.
quotes: The reason is to keep my writing as authentic and untainted as possible. It must be based on what I see, what I experience, and what I have success using myself.
The Oxygen Advantage explains how to breathe in such a way that avoids the physical manifestations of stress, which in turn calms the mind and eliminates anxiety.
It also played sweet music into my disdain and rejection of extrinsic rewards .
Essentialism made me take a hard look at how I was spending my time and empowered me to double-down on what matters most in my life and has the greatest positive influence on others.
But this book makes the case through mountains of research into performance that the way a skill is practiced and learned makes a huge difference in success.
